meta.blurb: A golden beetle, a dirty scrap of parchment and a friend who suddenly stops talking. William Legrand has found something on that paper and will not say what. Weeks later he orders spades and calls his friend to a hill at night.
meta.bible: William Legrand: an educated, moody man of old Huguenot family, once rich, now poor, who lives in a hut on Sullivan's Island and collects shells and insects. Jupiter: Legrand's old servant, freed long ago, loyal, brave but afraid of the beetle, who calls Legrand his young master. Narrator: Legrand's friend from Charleston, who tells the story in the first person. Wolf: Legrand's large Newfoundland dog. Lieutenant G: an officer at Fort Moultrie who borrows the beetle. Sullivan's Island: a thin strip of sand and myrtle bushes about three miles long, near Charleston, South Carolina. Fort Moultrie: the fort at the western end of the island. New Orleans: where Legrand's family came from. Huguenot: a French Protestant family. Captain Kidd: the pirate whose treasure is thought to be buried on the Atlantic coast. Bessop's Castle: a high rock four miles north of the island, from the old Bessop family; the message calls it the Bishop's Hotel. Facts: the beetle is gold-coloured with three black spots; the parchment shows a skull, a kid and a red cipher when warmed; the tree is a tulip tree and the skull is nailed to the seventh limb; the treasure chest holds more than four hundred and fifty thousand dollars in gold coin, a hundred and ten diamonds, eighteen rubies, three hundred and ten emeralds, twenty-one sapphires, an opal, and about a million and a half dollars in all; two skeletons lie in the pit. Voice and tone: a first-person adventure with a clever puzzle, warm humour and growing excitement; a dark detail about the skeletons is stated plainly, with no gore.

A1A2: Sullivan's Island is a long, narrow strip of sand near Charleston.
William Legrand lived in a hut with his old servant Jupiter.
One cold October evening, I walked to Legrand's hut.
Soon Legrand and Jupiter came in and welcomed me warmly.
The beetle was gold in colour, and Jupiter said it was gold.
Legrand had no paper, so he drew on a dirty scrap.
I looked at the drawing, and it looked like a skull.
Legrand looked closely at the paper, and his face changed.
A month later, Jupiter brought me a note from Legrand.
Jupiter put the new tools for digging in the boat.
Legrand looked pale, and he said the beetle was gold.
Legrand asked me to come with him into the hills.
We left at four, and Legrand swung the beetle on a string.
We climbed a hill and found a very tall tree.
Legrand told Jupiter to climb the tree with the beetle.
Jupiter climbed high into the tree, up to the first fork.
Jupiter went to the seventh limb, which was nearly dead.
At the end of the branch, Jupiter found a skull.
Legrand told Jupiter to drop the beetle through the left eye.
Legrand put a peg in the ground where the beetle fell.
We dug for two hours, but we found nothing.
As we left, Legrand suddenly seized Jupiter by the collar.
Jupiter pointed to his right eye, and Legrand shouted for joy.
Legrand moved the peg a little and measured again.
The dog found old bones and some gold and silver coins.
I tripped on an iron ring and found a big chest.
We opened the chest and saw gold and jewels shining.
Jupiter put his arms deep into the gold and smiled.
The chest was very heavy, so we took out most of the gold.
Most of the coins were gold, and they were very old.
There were also hundreds of jewels and many gold objects.
Legrand now explained how he had solved the mystery.
The scrap was parchment, and a skull was on it.
Legrand found the beetle near an old wrecked boat.
Jupiter wrapped the beetle in the scrap, and Legrand took it.
A skull is the sign of pirates, Legrand said.
The fire had made the skull appear on the parchment.
Heat showed a picture of a young goat on the parchment.
Everyone told stories about treasure buried by Captain Kidd.
Red marks and numbers slowly appeared on the warm parchment.
Legrand knew the signs were a secret code.
Legrand counted the signs and found the word the.
Soon he could read words like tree, through, and degree.
At last, the message told where the treasure lay.
Legrand searched for the bishop's hotel and found a rock.
On the rock, Legrand found a ledge shaped like a chair.
The next day, Legrand found the tree alone.
Jupiter dropped the beetle through the wrong eye.
Legrand had played a little joke on me.
Nobody knew who the two dead men in the hole were.
B1B2: Sullivan's Island lies near Charleston, South Carolina, and it is little more than a long strip of sea sand. It is about three miles long and less than a quarter of a mile wide, and sweet myrtle bushes cover most of it.
William Legrand was once rich, but he is poor now, and he lives in a small hut among the bushes. His old servant Jupiter, who was freed long ago, will never leave him.
In the middle of October there comes a day of unusual cold, and just before sunset I walk out to Legrand's hut. I live in Charleston, nine miles away, and I have not seen him for several weeks.

Soon after dark my hosts arrive and give me a warm welcome, and Jupiter bustles about to cook some marsh hens. Legrand is in one of his excited moods, because he has found a strange shell and a beetle that he thinks nobody knows.
Legrand says it is bright gold and as big as a hickory nut, with black spots on its back. Jupiter insists that the bug is solid gold, inside and out, and that he has never felt such a heavy one.

Legrand wants to show me the shape of the beetle, but he cannot find any paper in his drawer. He takes a dirty scrap from his waistcoat pocket and draws on it, and his big dog bursts in and jumps up at me.
When I look at the drawing, it looks more like a skull than an insect. Legrand replies that the black spots do look like eyes, but he is annoyed when I tell him he is no artist.

Legrand is about to crumple the paper and throw it into the fire when something in the drawing catches his eye. His face goes red and then pale, and he studies it for a long time by candlelight before locking it in his desk.

About a month later Jupiter comes to Charleston, looking worried, and says that his master is pale and silent and keeps drawing strange figures. He believes that the gold-bug has bitten Legrand, and he brings a note asking me to come at once.

The note sounds nothing like Legrand, and it worries me, so I decide to go with Jupiter at once. At the wharf I see a scythe and three new spades in the boat, and Jupiter says that his master told him to buy them.
At the hut I find Legrand pale, with glowing eyes, and he grasps my hand with nervous energy. He says the beetle is real gold and will make his fortune, and he brings it to me from a glass case.

Legrand says that he and Jupiter are going on an expedition into the hills, and that he needs someone he can trust. I think he is ill, but I finally agree, after he promises to follow my advice as his doctor once it is over.

We set out at about four o'clock, Legrand, Jupiter, the dog and I. Jupiter carries the tools, and Legrand swings the beetle on a cord like a magician and answers every question with only “we shall see”.

We cross the creek, walk northwest through wild country, and reach a high, wooded hill as the sun is setting. Jupiter cuts a path through the brambles with the scythe to the foot of a giant tulip tree.
Legrand asks Jupiter if he can climb the tree, and the old man walks around it and says that he can climb any tree. He is afraid of the beetle, but he agrees to carry it up on a string.

Jupiter hugs the huge trunk with his arms and knees and slowly climbs, until he reaches the first great fork high above the ground. Legrand tells him to follow the largest branch on this side and to count the limbs below him.
Legrand tells Jupiter to climb one limb higher, and soon he has reached the seventh limb. Legrand wants him to crawl out along it, but Jupiter is afraid, because the limb is nearly dead.

Legrand promises Jupiter a silver dollar if he goes out as far as he safely can without dropping the beetle. Near the end of the limb Jupiter cries out in surprise, because he has found a skull nailed to the tree.

Legrand tells Jupiter to find the left eye of the skull and to let the beetle drop through it on its string. Jupiter is confused about left and right, but at last he lowers the beetle, and it hangs shining in the evening light.
Legrand drives a peg into the ground at the exact spot where the beetle fell. He fastens a tape measure to the tree trunk, runs it past the peg for fifty feet, and marks a circle to dig in.
We light the lanterns and dig steadily for two hours, and the dog barks so loudly that Jupiter ties his mouth shut. We reach a depth of five feet, and then of seven, but we find nothing at all.

At last Legrand climbs out of the pit, bitterly disappointed, and puts on his coat, and we turn for home. After about a dozen steps he suddenly seizes Jupiter by the collar and demands to know which is his left eye.
Jupiter, very afraid, covers his right eye and says that it is his left. Legrand lets him go and dances about with joy, because he has found the mistake and the game is not over.

Jupiter says the beetle went through the eye that he took for the left, which was really the right. Legrand moves the peg three inches to the west, measures fifty feet again, and marks a new spot several yards from the first hole.
We dig again, and now I am strangely excited, because Legrand seems to have a plan. After an hour and a half, the dog howls and tears at the earth, uncovering two skeletons, a knife and some coins.

At the sight of the coins Jupiter can hardly control his joy, but Legrand looks disappointed. Then I stumble over a large iron ring in the earth, and we quickly dig out a heavy wooden chest bound with iron.

Our best efforts cannot move the chest, but its lid is held by only two sliding bolts. We draw them back with trembling hands, and a glittering heap of gold and jewels dazzles our eyes in the lantern light.

Jupiter is pale and stunned, and then he kneels in the pit and buries his arms in the gold up to the elbows. Quietly he says to himself that all this came from the beautiful gold-bug, and he is sorry that he was unkind to it.
We take out two thirds of the treasure and leave it in the bushes with the dog on guard. With great effort we carry the lighter chest home by one in the morning, and then we go back for the rest.

After a short sleep we spend a whole day and most of the next night sorting the treasure. In coins alone there is more than four hundred and fifty thousand dollars, all in old gold, with no American money.

There are also jewels of every kind, including a hundred and ten large diamonds, eighteen rubies, three hundred and ten emeralds and twenty-one sapphires. We also find rings, chains, crosses, a golden punch bowl and almost two hundred gold watches.

When the excitement has calmed, Legrand sees that I am dying of curiosity, and he begins to explain everything. He reminds me of the night when he made the rough sketch of the beetle and I said it looked like a skull.

When Legrand was about to throw the scrap into the fire, he saw that it was thin parchment, not paper. To his great surprise, he also saw a skull on the other side, in the very place where he had drawn the beetle.
That night Legrand thought carefully about how the parchment had come to him. He and Jupiter found the beetle on the coast about a mile east of the island, near the wreck of an old boat.
Jupiter picks up the scrap and wraps the beetle in it. On the way home they meet Lieutenant G, who takes the beetle, and Legrand puts the scrap in his own pocket without thinking.

Legrand had already joined two links of a chain: a boat on a seashore, and a parchment with a skull on it. A skull is the well-known sign of a pirate, and parchment is made to last, so he thought the scrap might hold something important.

Nobody had drawn the skull while Legrand sketched the beetle, so he thought of the fire. When the dog jumped up at me, I had let the parchment fall close to the flames, and the heat had brought out the skull.

Legrand heats the whole parchment, and in the corner opposite the skull he sees a small animal, a young goat called a kid. He thinks of the pirate Captain Kidd and takes the picture as a kind of signature.

Everyone has heard stories of treasure that Captain Kidd buried on the Atlantic coast. Legrand noticed that the stories were always about seekers and never about finders, and he decided that the treasure was still in the ground.
Legrand washes the dirty parchment with warm water and puts it on a hot tin pan over glowing charcoal. After a few minutes lines of strange signs appear in red, between the skull and the kid.

I tell Legrand that I cannot read the signs, but he says it is a simple code that any sailor could make. Because the joke on Kidd's name only works in English, he is sure that the message is in English.
Legrand counts how often each sign appears, and the commonest one must be e, the commonest letter in English. A group of three signs appears seven times, and it must spell the.
With the first words known, he guessed other words one by one. He found tree, then through, then degree and thirteen, and each new word gave him more letters of the key.

At last the whole message could be read, and it spoke of a good glass, a bishop's hostel and a devil's seat. It also told the finder to shoot from the left eye of a death's-head and to measure fifty feet.

Legrand divides the message into parts, and then he looks everywhere for a Bishop's Hotel. At last he remembers an old family named Bessop, and an old woman shows him the way to Bessop's Castle, a high rock.

On the face of the rock, Legrand finds a narrow ledge shaped like a chair, which must be the devil's seat. He hurries home for a telescope, points it as the message says, and sees a skull in a distant tree.

When Legrand leaves the rock, the round gap in the leaves vanishes, and he can see it only from that narrow ledge. Next morning he slips away from Jupiter and finds the tree after hard work, and Jupiter, who has been worried, even threatens to beat him.
Jupiter dropped the beetle through the right eye of the skull, and not the left. That made a difference of about two and a half inches at the peg, and over fifty feet it grew into several yards.
I ask why Legrand swung the beetle and dropped it from the tree, instead of a bullet. He answers that he was annoyed because I thought him mad, so he decided to tease me a little.
One question remains about the two skeletons in the pit, and Legrand can only guess. He thinks that Kidd may have killed his helpers when the work was done, which is a dreadful thing to believe.
C1C2: Many years ago I made the friendship of a man named William Legrand, who had retreated to Sullivan's Island, a strange sliver of sea sand near Charleston in South Carolina. The island is about three miles long and nowhere wider than a quarter of a mile, and it is separated from the mainland by a scarcely visible creek that winds through reeds and slime. Almost nothing grows there but a dense tangle of sweet myrtle, which in places rises fifteen or twenty feet and fills the air with its fragrance.

Legrand came of an ancient Huguenot family and had once been wealthy, but a series of misfortunes had reduced him to want. He had left New Orleans to escape the shame of it, and deep in the myrtle thicket he had built a small hut, where he lived among his books, his fishing lines and his collection of shells and insects. He was well educated and had unusual powers of mind, though his moods swung between wild enthusiasm and gloom, and he went everywhere with Jupiter, an old servant freed long before who would never leave his young master.

About the middle of October there came a day of remarkable chilliness, and just before sunset I scrambled through the evergreens to my friend's hut, which I had not visited for several weeks. I lived in Charleston, nine miles from the island, and the means of crossing were far poorer then than they are today. Getting no answer to my knock, I found the key where it was always hidden, let myself in, and settled beside a fine fire that was blazing on the hearth.

They arrived soon after dark and gave me a most cordial welcome, while Jupiter, grinning from ear to ear, bustled about preparing marsh hens for supper. Legrand was in one of his fits of enthusiasm, for he had found an unknown shellfish that formed a new genus, and had also hunted down, with Jupiter's help, a scarabaeus that he believed to be entirely new. He wished to have my opinion of it in the morning, he said, because he had foolishly lent it to Lieutenant G from the fort.

It was of a brilliant gold colour, Legrand told me, about the size of a large hickory nut, with two jet-black spots near one end of its back and a longer one near the other. Jupiter broke in to insist that it was solid gold, every bit of it, wings excepted, and that he had never in his life felt so heavy a bug. Legrand admitted, rather more earnestly than the occasion demanded, that the lustre of its scales was almost enough to justify the old man's opinion.

Wishing to show me its shape, Legrand sat at a table that held pen and ink but no paper, and after searching a drawer in vain he drew a scrap of dirty foolscap from his waistcoat pocket. He made a rough drawing on it with the pen and handed it to me while I sat by the fire, for I was still chilly. Just then a loud growl and a scratching at the door announced Legrand's large Newfoundland, which rushed in, leaped upon my shoulders, and loaded me with caresses.

After studying it for some minutes I confessed that this was a strange scarabaeus indeed, and that it more nearly resembled a skull, or death's-head, than anything else I had ever seen. Legrand replied, with some warmth, that on paper it might look a little like that, since the two upper spots could be eyes and the longer one a mouth. When I teased him that he was no artist, and that I should have to wait for the beetle itself, he became visibly nettled and insisted that he had had good masters and drew tolerably well.

Taking the paper back, Legrand grew peevish and was about to crumple it into the fire when a casual glance at the design seemed suddenly to rivet his attention, and his face turned violently red and then excessively pale. He carried a candle to a sea-chest in the farthest corner of the room, turned the paper in every direction, and examined it with anxious care, saying nothing at all. At last he placed it in a wallet, locked the wallet in a writing-desk, and fell into such a reverie that I thought it kinder to take my leave.

About a month later Jupiter came to Charleston to visit me, looking more dispirited than I had ever seen him, and I feared that some disaster had befallen my friend. He told me, in great distress, that his master was not well, though he complained of nothing, for he went about pale and with his head down, and he kept covering a slate with the queerest figures. Jupiter was sure that the golden beetle had bitten his master, who dreamed of gold and talked of it in his sleep, and he handed me a note begging me to come at once.

The tone of the note was so unlike Legrand that I dreaded the pressure of misfortune had unsettled his reason, and without a moment's hesitation I prepared to go with Jupiter. At the wharf I noticed a scythe and three spades, all apparently new, lying in the bottom of the boat in which we were to sail. Jupiter explained that his master had ordered him to buy them in town, at what he thought a ridiculous price, and he added that all of it was because of the bug.

We reached the hut about three in the afternoon, and Legrand seized my hand with a nervous warmth that alarmed me, for his face was ghastly pale and his deep-set eyes glared with an unnatural brightness. He told me, with profound seriousness, that Jupiter was right about the beetle, for it was a bug of real gold that would make his fortune and restore him to his family's possessions. He then brought it from a glass case, a beautiful insect, unknown to naturalists at that time, and so heavy that I could hardly blame Jupiter for his opinion.

I urged him to go to bed and let me watch over him, but he insisted that he was as well as could be expected under such excitement, and that I could help him only by relieving it. He and Jupiter were going on an expedition into the hills, he explained, and they needed someone they could trust, whether they succeeded or failed. After a struggle I agreed to go, provided that when this freak was over he would go home and follow my advice implicitly, as that of his physician.

We started about four o'clock, Legrand, Jupiter, the dog and I, and Jupiter insisted on carrying the scythe and the spades, more through fear of leaving them within his master's reach than through any love of work. I carried a couple of dark lanterns, while Legrand contented himself with the beetle, which he twirled to and fro on the end of a bit of whip-cord with the air of a conjuror. I could scarcely refrain from tears at this plain evidence of my friend's confusion, and to every question about the purpose of our journey he replied only that we should see.

We crossed the creek and journeyed northwest for about two hours through a wild and desolate country, with Legrand leading the way and pausing here and there to consult landmarks of his own making. As the sun was setting we reached a dreary tableland near the summit of an almost inaccessible hill, densely wooded and strewn with huge crags. Jupiter, at his master's direction, hacked a path through the brambles to the foot of an enormous tulip tree that stood among eight or ten oaks and surpassed them all in beauty of form and spread of branches.

Legrand asked Jupiter whether he could climb it, and the old man, a little staggered, walked slowly around the huge trunk, examined it with minute attention, and replied that he could climb any tree he had ever seen. Legrand then told him to take the beetle up with him, and Jupiter, drawing back in dismay, protested that he did not want to carry the bug up the tree at all. Only when Legrand called it a harmless dead beetle, to be carried by a string, did the old man take hold of the cord, holding the insect as far from himself as he could.

Embracing the great trunk with his arms and knees, and resting his bare toes on any bumps he could find, Jupiter wriggled his way into the first fork, sixty or seventy feet above the ground. Legrand told him to keep to the largest branch on that side, and the old man obeyed so promptly that he soon vanished among the thick leaves. Presently his voice was heard calling down that he could see the sky through the top of the tree, and that he had already passed five big limbs on that side.

Counting five big limbs passed, Jupiter was ordered to go one limb higher, and a few minutes later he announced that he had reached the seventh. Legrand, evidently much excited, told him to work his way out along it as far as he could and to report anything strange, while I, by now persuaded that my friend was mad, could think only of getting him home. Jupiter, however, called down that the limb was dead almost all the way, and when Legrand asked anxiously whether he was sure, the old man tested the wood with his knife and found it rotten, though not too rotten.

Jupiter suggested dropping the heavy beetle first, but Legrand cried that he would break his neck if it fell, and offered a silver dollar for going as far as he safely could while holding the string. Soon the old man was almost at the end of the limb, and then he gave a sudden cry of alarm, for upon the tree he had found a skull. Someone had left a head up there, he said, and the crows had picked it clean, and a large nail through the skull held it fast to the limb.

Legrand ordered him to find the left eye of the skull, and after a long, puzzled pause, in which Jupiter wondered which side the skull's left hand was on, the old man announced that he had found it. The beetle descended slowly on its cord, glistening like a globe of burnished gold in the last rays of the setting sun, and hung clear of the branches, so that it would have fallen at our feet. Legrand took up the scythe and cleared a circular space three or four yards across beneath the insect, and then he told Jupiter to let go the string and come down.

Legrand drove a peg into the ground at the precise spot where the beetle had fallen, and fastened a tape measure to the point of the trunk nearest the peg. He unrolled it past the peg for fifty feet in a straight line while Jupiter cleared away the brambles, and at the end he drove a second peg and drew a rough circle four feet across. Then he gave a spade to Jupiter and another to me, took one himself, and begged us to begin digging as quickly as possible.

I had no relish for the work, but I saw no way to escape without upsetting my poor friend, and so I resolved to dig with a good will and convince the visionary, by plain demonstration, of his folly. We dug steadily for two hours by lantern light, saying little, while the dog's yelping grew so loud that Jupiter climbed out, tied up the animal's mouth with one of his suspenders, and returned to his task. When we had reached a depth of five feet, and then of seven, and still no treasure had appeared, Legrand, though plainly disconcerted, wiped his brow and began to dig again.

At last the gold-seeker, whom I sincerely pitied, clambered from the pit with the bitterest disappointment on his face, put on the coat that he had thrown off at the start, and reluctantly gave the signal to go home. We had taken perhaps a dozen steps in silence when Legrand strode up to Jupiter, seized him by the collar, and demanded, between clenched teeth, to be told without delay which was his left eye. The astonished old man dropped the spades and fell on his knees, and then, in terror, clapped his hand over his right eye, as if afraid that his master meant to gouge it out.

Legrand let him go and, shouting that he had known it all along, executed a series of leaps and capers, much to the astonishment of his servant, who looked mutely from his master to me. The game was not up yet, he announced, and he led the way back to the tulip tree. There he asked Jupiter whether the skull had been nailed to the limb with its face outward or toward the branch, and learned that it had faced outward.

Jupiter admitted that he had dropped the beetle through the eye he thought was his left, and as he spoke he touched his right eye once more. Legrand, satisfied, moved the peg about three inches to the westward of its first position, drew the tape from the nearest point of the trunk to it, and extended the line to a distance of fifty feet. This marked a spot several yards from the place where we had been digging, and around it he described a slightly larger circle, and we began to work with the spades again.

I was dreadfully weary, but I no longer disliked the labour, for something in Legrand's air of forethought had impressed me, and I caught myself looking, almost with expectation, for the treasure that had turned my friend's wits. After about an hour and a half the dog's howling, which had begun in play, took on a bitter and serious tone, and he leaped into the hole and tore up the earth with his claws. In a few seconds he had uncovered two complete skeletons, with metal buttons and the dust of decayed wool, and the spade soon turned up a large Spanish knife and some loose coins of gold and silver.

At the sight of the coins Jupiter could scarcely restrain his joy, but Legrand looked disappointed and urged us on, and he had hardly spoken when I stumbled over a large iron ring half buried in the earth. We now worked in earnest, and I have never passed ten minutes in more intense excitement, for in that time we had unearthed an oblong wooden chest, remarkably well preserved and as hard as stone. It was firmly secured by bands of wrought iron, riveted into a kind of open trellis, and on each side it had three iron rings by which six people could lift it.

Our united efforts served only to shift the chest slightly in its bed, and we saw at once that we could not lift so great a weight, but luckily the lid was fastened only by two sliding bolts. We drew them back, trembling and panting with anxiety, and in an instant a treasure of incalculable value lay gleaming before us, as the lantern light fell upon a confused heap of gold and jewels that dazzled our eyes. I shall not pretend to describe my feelings, since amazement was predominant, and Legrand appeared exhausted by excitement and spoke hardly a word.

Jupiter's face wore the pallor of a man thunderstruck, and presently he fell upon his knees in the pit and buried his arms to the elbows in the gold, as if he enjoyed the luxury of a bath. At length, with a deep sigh, he said to himself that all this had come from the pretty gold-bug, the poor little gold-bug that he had treated in such a savage fashion. He asked himself, and received no answer, whether he was not thoroughly ashamed of the way he had treated the little creature.

It was growing late, and I had to rouse master and servant to the need of moving the treasure before daylight. We lightened the chest by taking out two thirds of its contents, which we left among the brambles with the dog standing guard, and then we hauled the chest home, reaching the hut at one in the morning. After a short rest and a supper we returned to the hills with three stout sacks, shared out the remainder of the booty, and reached the hut again just as dawn was breaking.

The chest had been full to the brim, with everything heaped in anyhow, and we spent that whole day and much of the night sorting it, finding ourselves richer than we had dared to suppose. In coin there was rather more than four hundred and fifty thousand dollars, and there was not a particle of silver, only gold of antique date, French, Spanish and German, with a few English guineas. There was no American money at all, and several very large and heavy coins were so worn that we could make nothing of their inscriptions.

The jewels were harder to value, for they included a hundred and ten diamonds, eighteen rubies, three hundred and ten emeralds, twenty-one sapphires and an opal, all broken from their settings. Besides these there were nearly two hundred massive rings and earrings, about thirty rich chains, eighty-three heavy crucifixes, five gold censers, a prodigious punch bowl, and a hundred and ninety-seven superb gold watches. We estimated the whole contents of the chest that night at a million and a half of dollars, and when the jewels were later sold, it proved that we had greatly undervalued the treasure.

When the first excitement had subsided, Legrand, who saw that I was dying with impatience for a solution of this extraordinary riddle, entered into a full account of every circumstance connected with it. He reminded me of the night when he handed me his rough sketch of the scarabaeus, and of how he had been vexed that I insisted it resembled a death's-head. At first he had thought I was joking, he said, but then he had remembered the peculiar spots on the insect's back and admitted that my remark had some foundation, although my sneer at his drawing had still stung.

As he was crumpling it to throw it into the fire, Legrand explained, his glance fell on the sketch, and he saw to his amazement the figure of a death's-head just where he thought he had drawn the beetle. The scrap, he now realised, was not paper but very thin parchment, and when he turned it over he found his own drawing on the reverse side, exactly as he had made it. He was certain that there had been no skull on the parchment when he drew, for he had turned it over in search of the cleanest spot, and the discovery left him stupefied with astonishment.

That night, when Jupiter was fast asleep, Legrand set about a more methodical study of the affair, beginning with the manner in which the parchment had come to him. The beetle had been found on the mainland coast, about a mile east of the island, and when Legrand took hold of it, it gave him a sharp bite, and he let it drop. Jupiter, before seizing it, looked about for a leaf, and his eyes and Legrand's fell on a corner of parchment sticking up out of the sand, near the remains of what seemed a ship's long boat.

Jupiter picked up the parchment, wrapped the beetle in it, and gave it to his master, and soon afterwards they met Lieutenant G, who begged to take the insect to the fort. When Legrand consented, the lieutenant thrust it into his waistcoat pocket without the parchment, which Legrand went on holding in his hand, and he must have put it into his own pocket without knowing it. That was why, when he went to the table to sketch the beetle and found no paper in the drawer, his hand fell upon the parchment in his pocket.

Already, Legrand said, he had put together two links of a great chain, for there was a boat on a seacoast and, near it, a parchment with a skull, the well-known emblem of the pirate. Parchment, moreover, is almost imperishable, and matters of little moment are rarely written on it, so he judged that the scrap had been chosen for a record meant to be long preserved. He also noticed that, although one corner had been destroyed, its oblong shape was just such as might have been chosen for a memorandum.

When he had drawn the beetle there had been no skull, and since I had returned the sketch to him and no one else was present, it could not have been drawn by any human hand, yet there it was. Then he remembered that the weather had been chilly, a fire had been blazing, and that when the dog leaped upon my shoulders I had let the parchment fall between my knees close to the flames. Heat, he concluded, had brought out the skull, since certain chemical preparations make writing visible only when warmed, and it fades again as the material cools.

At once Legrand heated every part of the parchment, and in the corner diagonally opposite the death's-head there appeared the figure of what he took for a goat but soon decided was a kid. He thought of one Captain Kidd, and at once took the animal for a kind of pun or picture-signature, while the skull at the other corner seemed to him a stamp or seal. What puzzled him was the absence of everything else, the body of the document that should lie between the seal and the signature.

He had heard, like everyone, the rumours of money buried on the Atlantic coast by Kidd and his companions, and he reasoned that stories so long repeated could have lasted only if the treasure was still hidden. The tales, he pointed out, were all about money-seekers and never about money-finders, for had the pirate dug up his plunder, the matter would have dropped. Some accident, perhaps the loss of a note of where it lay, must have robbed Kidd of the means of recovering it, and Legrand began to hope, almost to believe, that the parchment was that lost record.

A second heating at first produced nothing, so Legrand wondered whether the dirt was to blame, and he rinsed the parchment in warm water and laid it, skull downward, in a tin pan over lighted charcoal. In a few minutes the pan was thoroughly hot, and when he removed the slip he found it spotted in several places with what seemed to be figures arranged in lines. After one more minute over the fire the whole message was visible, traced in a red tint between the death's-head and the kid, and he held it out for me to see.

I returned the slip to him, saying that I was as much in the dark as ever, but the solution, Legrand replied, was by no means so difficult as it looked. The signs formed a cipher, and from what was known of Kidd he could not imagine the pirate making any very abstruse one, only a simple kind that would seem unsolvable to a rough sailor without the key. The pun on the name Kidd, he added, works only in English, so he assumed from the start that the message was written in that language.

There were no divisions between the words, Legrand said, which would have made the task far easier, so his first step was to count the signs and find which were used most. The one that looked like an eight occurred thirty-three times, more than any other, and since e is the commonest letter in English, he took that sign to stand for e. Then he searched for the commonest word in the language, which is the, and found one group of three signs, ending in the sign for e, that appeared no fewer than seven times.

Having established one word, Legrand explained, he could mark the beginnings and endings of other words, and by trying each letter in the gaps he read first the tree, then through the, and later degree and thirteen. At the very beginning of the message the first two words proved to be a good, which told him that the first letter was a. In this way the key grew letter by letter, until he had found no fewer than eleven of the most important letters, and he said that the rest was only a matter of patience.

When the key was complete the message could be read, and it spoke of a good glass, a bishop's hostel and a devil's seat, of forty-one degrees and thirteen minutes, and of the seventh limb of the main branch. It ended with an order to shoot from the left eye of the death's-head, and to take a straight line from the tree through the shot, fifty feet out. I confessed that the riddle seemed as dark as ever, and Legrand admitted that it still wore a serious look when regarded with a casual glance.

His first task, Legrand said, was to divide the message into its natural parts, which he did by noticing five places where the writer had crowded his signs unusually close together. Then he spent several days asking about a building called the Bishop's Hotel, until it occurred to him that the name might refer to an old family, the Bessops, who owned a manor-house four miles to the north. At the plantation one of the oldest women said that she knew a Bessop's Castle, though it was neither a castle nor a tavern but a high rock, and for a fee she guided him to it.

A little below the summit, on the eastern face, Legrand saw a narrow ledge which, with the help of a niche above it, looked like a hollow-backed chair, and he felt sure that this was the devil's seat. A good glass, he knew, could mean only a telescope, and the degrees and the compass direction were plainly meant to aim it, so he hurried home, fetched one, and returned to the rock. Seated on the ledge, he aimed the glass as the message directed and found, in a circular opening among the leaves of a large tree, a white spot that proved to be a human skull.

The circular opening vanished the instant Legrand left the devil's seat, and repeated experiment showed that it could be seen from no other point than that narrow ledge, which he thought the chief ingenuity of the whole business. Jupiter had come with him to the rock and had been watching him anxiously for some weeks, but early next morning Legrand contrived to give him the slip and went alone into the hills to look for the tree. After much toil he found it, and when he came home that night, his servant, who had spent the day in worry, proposed to give him a flogging.

I guessed that we had missed the spot because Jupiter let the beetle fall through the right eye instead of the left, and Legrand agreed, saying that it shifted the peg by about two and a half inches. Had the treasure lain beneath that peg, the error would have mattered little, but the peg and the trunk were only two points on a line, so the small mistake grew larger with every foot. By the time we had measured fifty feet it had thrown us quite off the scent, and only Legrand's deep belief that treasure lay buried somewhere had kept us from giving up.

I asked why he had behaved so strangely, swinging the beetle about and insisting on dropping it from the skull instead of a bullet. To be frank, Legrand replied, he had been annoyed by my obvious doubts about his sanity, and had resolved to punish me quietly with a little sober mystification. That was why he had swung the beetle and let it fall from the tree, an idea that had come to him from my own remark about how heavy it was.

As for the two skeletons in the pit, Legrand said, he could no more explain them than I could, though there seemed only one plausible account, and it was dreadful to believe in so great an atrocity. Kidd, if it was indeed Kidd who hid the treasure, must have had help in the labour, and when the work was done he may have thought it wise to remove everyone who shared his secret. Perhaps a couple of blows with a mattock were enough while his helpers were busy in the pit, or perhaps it took a dozen, and who can say.
